title: Ganesha writes the Mahabharata
hookLine: a poet needs a scribe, and the lord of beginnings takes the pen: why Hindus start with Ganesha
carry: ganesha comes first, at every beginning
last: ASKING IS PART OF THE PATH.

lines: A POET WHO NEEDS A SCRIBE.
cards: A poet has a story too long to write down himself, so he asks for a scribe. The one who comes is Ganesha.
Tradition tells it this way: Vyasa has the Mahabharata in his mind, and Ganesha agrees to write it on one condition. Once the pen starts, it must not stop.
Vyasa agrees, and adds a condition of his own: Ganesha must understand every line before he writes it. A good story for the last day of year four, with year five starting tomorrow, with letters.

teach.b: Why Ganesha? Because in Hindu practice he comes first. Before a wedding, a puja, a journey, a new house or a new school year, families honor Ganesha before anyone else.
He's lord of obstacles, the one who clears them, and in some stories the one who sets them in the path of the proud. He's lord of beginnings, and patron of learning and letters.
So it fits that the greatest of the epics begins with him bent over a page. And the bargain is worth hearing. Ganesha's condition: no stopping.
Vyasa's: nothing written that isn't understood. Tradition adds that whenever Vyasa needed time, he'd recite a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to pause to work it out.
Then the broken tusk. In some tellings, Ganesha's pen breaks mid-story, and rather than break his word, he snaps off his own tusk and keeps writing.
That's one reason many images show him with one tusk broken, sometimes holding it like a pen. Other stories explain the tusk differently; this one is the scribe's.
And it's why many Hindus write Shri Ganeshaya Namah, salutations to Lord Ganesha, at the top of a first page: a letter, an exam, a new account book at Diwali. Not as a charm.

As a way of saying this work is offered, from its first line. Next year opens with Sanskrit for readers: the script, a few sacred words, enough to look at a verse and know it. A scribe's kind of year.
It's right to begin it with Ganesha.

games.q: you're starting something new: a first day at work, the first page of a notebook. what does Hindu practice put first?
o: Ganesha: a short prayer, or Shri Ganeshaya Namah at the top of the page.
nothing yet. prayers come at the end, once it's gone well.
whichever god you like best that day.
games.why: Ganesha comes first. the lord of beginnings, who took the pen for the Mahabharata, is honored at the start of new work.

practice: Begin the way many Hindus begin anything. Hands together, and silently, Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, or simply: Ganesha, be with this beginning.
Then, with one fingertip, trace a slow line on your palm, as if writing a single letter, one stroke to a breath. If the mind runs ahead to next year, bring it back to this one line.
If you don't pray, let the first stroke be your way of saying: this is offered.

wordCard.voice: Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, now walked. And the ranges beyond, waiting. Today's word.
